sections.title: Core Foundations & Conceptual Framework
sections.content:
• **Centralized Autocracy**: The King (Raya) was the supreme authority, head of justice, and military commander, often claiming divine status (e.g., 'Hindu-raya-suratrana').
• **Nayankara System**: A military-feudal arrangement where 'Nayakas' were granted land (Amaram) in exchange for maintaining troops and paying tribute to the center.
• **Ayagar System**: A village-level administrative mechanism consisting of 12 hereditary officials (Ayagars) who managed local production, tax collection, and law and order.
• **Key Metric / Factor**: The 'Sist' (land revenue) was the primary source of state income, usually fixed at 1/6th of the produce, though it varied based on land fertility and irrigation.

sections.title: Comprehensive Classification & Comparative Matrix
rows: Decentralized military control; obligation to provide troops.
High-yield: Often compared with Delhi Sultanate's Iqta system.
Local autonomy; tax collection and record keeping.
Prelims: Frequently asked about the role of 'Karnam' (accountant).
Direct control of the King over administrative records.
Mains: Shows the sophistication of the bureaucratic apparatus.

items.title: Major Applications / Initiatives
items.content:
• **Temple-Centric Economy**: Temples acted as banks, employers, and centers of land management, reinforcing state legitimacy.
• **Irrigation Policy**: State-sponsored construction of tanks and canals to boost agricultural revenue (e.g., Tungabhadra river projects).

items.title: Challenges & Way Forward
items.content:
• **Key Challenges**: Growing independence of Nayakas leading to political fragmentation post-Talikota.
• **Solutions**: Centralized oversight via the 'Rayasam' and periodic inspection of Nayaka accounts.

items.title: Mnemonic for Retention
items.content:
• **Memory Acronym**: 'NAK' (Nayaka, Ayagar, Karnam).
• **Decoded Meaning**: N (Nayaka = Military/Land), A (Ayagar = Village/Local), K (Karnam = Accountant/Record).

upscNotes.content: Examiner Trap: UPSC often confuses 'Nayankara' with 'Iqtadari'. While similar, Nayankara was more hereditary and focused on military-feudal land grants, whereas Iqta was theoretically non-hereditary and administrative.
Mains Value Addition: Use the term 'Segmentary State' (coined by Burton Stein) to describe the Vijayanagar polity, highlighting the tension between central authority and local Nayaka power.

keyTakeaways: The Nayankara system was the backbone of the military-feudal structure.
The Ayagar system ensured village-level stability and revenue collection.
Temples were not just religious sites but vital administrative and economic hubs.
